AIT Special Study · report as of 11 November 2026

The Special Study, in plain words

How well can simple, standard methods forecast satellite soil moisture a few days ahead, at one place in Pathum Thani? This guide explains the report, so that you can explain it to others.

  • 129pages in the report
  • 1selected grid cell
  • 2, 3, 5, 8days ahead
  • 981days with a usable reading, in 9 years

สรุปสั้น

  • งานนี้วัดว่า "โมเดลมาตรฐาน" พยากรณ์ความชื้นผิวดินจากดาวเทียม SMAP ล่วงหน้า 2, 3, 5 และ 8 วัน ได้ดีแค่ไหน ที่ช่องกริดช่องเดียวในปทุมธานี
  • ข้อมูลดาวเทียมที่ "คุณภาพดี" ไม่มีเลยในพื้นที่ที่ SMAP จัดเป็นเมือง ซึ่งคิดเป็น 76.2% ของจังหวัด จึงต้องเลือกช่องที่ไม่ใช่เมือง
  • วิธีง่ายที่สุดคือเอาค่า 3 ครั้งล่าสุดมาเฉลี่ย ก็ชนะวิธี "พรุ่งนี้เท่ากับวันนี้" แล้ว โมเดลเรียนรู้เพิ่มได้อีกนิดเดียวที่ 8 วัน (ประมาณ +0.06) และผลนี้ผ่านเกณฑ์แบบเฉียดฉิว
  • ข้อมูลเรดาร์ Sentinel-1 และข้อมูลอากาศไม่ช่วยให้ดีขึ้นแบบวัดได้
  • จุดอ่อนอยู่ที่ข้อมูล ไม่ใช่โมเดล: ช่องเดียว ไม่มีเซนเซอร์ภาคพื้นดิน และวันที่ดินเปียกที่สุดถูกตัดทิ้ง

The answer, in five findings

  1. Smoothing does most of the work.Just averaging the last three readings beats "tomorrow equals today" at every horizon.
  2. Learning adds a small gain at 8 days.Ridge regression adds +0.060 on top of that average: about 6% less error. It is small, and it sits close to the pass line of the strict test. Which model wins?
  3. Radar and weather add nothing measurable.Adding Sentinel-1 or weather changes skill by at most 0.02. That is "not measurable here", not "useless".
  4. Wetting after heavy rain is not forecast.No input knows about rain that has not fallen yet.
  5. A one-number rule is hard to beat."Seasonal normal plus a fixed share of the recent departure" scores as well as the learned models.

Understand it

How a forecast is made

In one lineA forecast is a guess at the next satellite reading, made only from what was known on the day it was issued. The study makes 1,710 such guesses with each method and scores them.

ภาษาไทยสั้น ๆ

  • การพยากรณ์หนึ่งครั้ง คือการทายว่าดาวเทียมจะอ่านค่าความชื้นได้เท่าไรในอีก 2, 3, 5 หรือ 8 วัน โดยใช้เฉพาะข้อมูลที่มีอยู่ ณ วันที่พยากรณ์
  • ลำดับงาน: เก็บค่าที่ดาวเทียมอ่านได้ → คัดเฉพาะค่าคุณภาพดี → จับคู่ "วันนี้" กับ "อีก h วัน" → สร้างตัวเลขอธิบายวันนี้ (อินพุต) → ให้โมเดลเรียนจากปีก่อน ๆ → ให้ทุกวิธีทายค่า → เทียบกับค่าจริงแล้วให้คะแนน
  • ตัวอย่างจริงในหน้านี้: พยากรณ์เมื่อ 2 ม.ค. 2024 สำหรับวันที่ 10 ม.ค. 2024 ค่าที่ดาวเทียมอ่านได้จริงคือ 0.336

  1. Collect the satellite readings

    SMAP passes over cell (3,6) on three days out of every eight. Each pass gives a reading: how wet the top 5 cm of soil is, as a number such as 0.369. That means 0.369 cubic metres of water in each cubic metre of soil. From 2016 to 2024 the cell has 2,376 readings.

  2. Keep only the readings NASA recommends

    Every reading carries a quality flag. Only those marked "recommended" are kept: 1,672 of the 2,376. The morning reading is used where there is one, otherwise the evening one. That leaves 981 days with a reading, out of 3,288 days.

  3. Pair each reading with the one that came later

    The later reading is the answer that the forecast will be judged against. A pair exists only when both readings exist, exactly 2, 3, 5 or 8 days apart.

    • 333pairs 2 days apart
    • 601pairs 3 days apart
    • 598pairs 5 days apart
    • 872pairs 8 days apart

  4. Describe the forecast day with numbers

    A model cannot look at a calendar or a map. It is handed a row of numbers, called the inputs. Here is the row for one real forecast: the first 8-day forecast of 2024.

    Worked exampleIssued 2 January 2024, for 10 January 2024 (8 days ahead)
    Latest reading, 2 Jan
    0.369
    Reading before, 30 Dec
    0.342 3 days old
    Two before, 28 Dec
    0.349 5 days old
    Three before, 25 Dec
    0.403 8 days old
    Season
    day 2 of the year
    Radar scene, same day
    −5.8 / −14.1 dB
    Rain, last 7 and 30 days
    0 / 2.3 mm
    Temperature, last 3 days
    28.3 °C

    The first five boxes are the nine inputs every model gets: four readings, three ages, and the season written as two numbers. Radar and weather are the optional extras.

  5. Learn from earlier years only

    For a forecast issued in 2024, the learned models are trained on the 761 pairs issued from 2016 to 2023. Their settings are picked by a rehearsal on 2023. Nothing from 2024 is seen until the test.

    201620172018201920202021202220232024

    The same is repeated for every test year from 2018 to 2024. This is called walk-forward testing.

  6. Every forecaster gives its number

    Each method now says what it expects the satellite to read on 10 January.

    In this one case the plain average came closest. That is fine. A single forecast shows how the machine works, not who wins.

  7. Score all the forecasts together

    At 8 days there are 639 test forecasts like this one, over seven test years. For each method the misses are combined into one typical error, called RMSE.

    • Skill turns the error into a share. The mean of three has an error 6.9% smaller than persistence, so its skill is +0.069. Ridge's skill is +0.125.
    • Gain over the mean of three is the same idea with the plain average as the reference. Ridge's error is 6.0% smaller than the mean of three's, so its gain is +0.060. That is the headline number of the report.
    • Tests then ask whether a difference of this size could be luck. See how solid the main result is.

What each model adds

In one lineAveraging the last three readings does most of the work. Learning adds a little on top at 8 days. Radar and weather add nothing measurable.

ภาษาไทยสั้น ๆ

  • วิธีที่ไม่ต้องเรียนรู้ เช่น ใช้ค่าล่าสุด หรือเฉลี่ย 3 ครั้งล่าสุด คือ "ไม้บรรทัด" ที่โมเดลต้องเอาชนะให้ได้
  • Ridge คือค่าเฉลี่ยถ่วงน้ำหนักที่โมเดลหาน้ำหนักเอง Random forest คือต้นไม้ตัดสินใจ 300 ต้นช่วยกันตอบ ส่วน XGBoost คือต้นไม้ 500 ต้นที่ต้นหลังคอยแก้ข้อผิดพลาดของต้นก่อน
  • ผลที่ได้: การเฉลี่ยให้ประโยชน์มากที่สุด การเรียนรู้เพิ่มได้เล็กน้อยที่ 8 วัน ส่วนเรดาร์และข้อมูลอากาศไม่ช่วยแบบวัดได้

Seven forecasters, simplest first

Four are simple references that use nothing but the readings. Three are learned models. The number at the foot of each card is its forecast in the worked example; the reading that arrived was 0.336.

simple reference

Persistence

"Tomorrow equals today." Copy the latest reading.

example: 0.369

simple reference

Seasonal normal

The usual value for this time of year, taken from earlier years within 7 days of the date.

example: 0.377

simple reference

Damped persistence

The latest reading, pulled part of the way back to the long-run average. The size of the pull is fitted on earlier years.

example: 0.377

simple reference

Mean of three

Average the last three readings. Nothing is fitted. This is the bar the learned models must clear.

example: 0.353

learned model

Ridge regression

A weighted sum of the inputs. The weights are learned from earlier years, and a penalty keeps them small.

example: 0.362

learned model

Random forest

300 decision trees. Each is a chain of yes-or-no questions about the inputs. Their answers are averaged.

example: 0.367

learned model

XGBoost

500 small trees built one after another. Each one corrects the mistakes left by those before it.

example: 0.364

How three of them weigh the last four readings

Persistence trusts only the latest reading. The mean of three trusts three equally. Ridge learned its own weights from the data.

In plain words, ridge is a cautious average. It leans most on the latest reading, less on older ones, and pulls the result toward what is normal for the time of year.

Inside the example: how ridge built its number

Because ridge only adds things up, its forecast can be taken apart exactly.

  • Start: the average of all past answers0.389
  • The four recent readings, mostly lower than usual−0.020
  • The time of year, early January−0.007
  • How old the earlier readings areabout 0
  • Ridge's forecast for 10 January0.362

Trees work differently

A tree never adds things up. It sorts the day into a group by asking questions, and answers with the average outcome of similar past days. That lets it bend where ridge cannot. It also means a tree cannot answer with a value wetter than anything it saw in training.

What each forecaster contributes

Skill is the share of persistence's error that a forecaster removes. Zero is persistence itself.

  • The mean of three already removes 7 to 20% of the error, with no learning at all.
  • The learned models sit close to it: mostly a little above at 3 and 8 days, below at 2 days.
  • The seasonal normal alone is not enough. It is worse than persistence at 2, 5 and 8 days.

What learning adds on top of the plain average

This is the fair test of a learned model: its gain over the mean of three. A shaded number passed the strict test, which allows for twelve comparisons being made.

Gain over the mean of three2 days3 days5 days8 days
Ridge regression−0.049+0.042−0.010+0.060
Random forest−0.090+0.040+0.032+0.081
XGBoost−0.235−0.016−0.007+0.054
  • Ridge at 8 days (+0.060) is the result the report stands on. It also passes when a few borderline training pairs are removed.
  • The random forest at 8 days (+0.081) passes in the main run only. A later check showed that it is sensitive to settings chosen on a single year.
  • Ridge at 3 days (+0.042) does not pass the strict test. The report calls it suggestive.

What radar and weather add

Each group of four bars is the same ridge model given more inputs. The bars barely move.

Say it carefully: no measurable additional information under the present data, quality filtering and evaluation protocol. It does not show that radar or weather are useless.

Why these three models, and not deep learning

Statisticalused here
Classic MLused here
Deep learningthesis
Transformersthesis
Graph networksthesis
Physics-informedthesis
Foundation modelsthesis
  • Each model asks a different question. Ridge: does a learned weighting beat fixed weights? Random forest: do curved effects add anything? XGBoost: does fitting harder add more? Together they run from simple to flexible.
  • Tree models are the usual baseline. A review of 144 studies found the random forest the most used and most often the best.
  • Deep learning is ahead only narrowly at short leads. In the largest like-for-like comparison (Wang et al. 2024, 5 cm depth), the random forest scored R² 0.924, 0.874 and 0.797 at 1, 3 and 7 days; the LSTM scored 0.943, 0.895 and 0.816.
  • Deep learning was left out on purpose. A test year is forecast from only 126 to 761 training pairs. A model whose behaviour cannot be checked on so few would spoil a clean reference. Deep models belong to the thesis.
  • The closest earlier study does not close the gap. Fang and Shen (2020) forecast SMAP L3 with an LSTM and report good errors, but persistence is not among their comparisons.
How these choices answer the gaps in the literature

The gap is not a missing clever model. It is a missing fair measurement: against a simple reference, with a test, in the tropics. Standard models scored strictly are what closes that.

Gap in the literatureWhat the study didThe report's own verdict
No benchmark against persistence for a tropical province on the edge of a cityPersistence, the seasonal normal and three learned models, tested year by year from 2016 to 2024.Partly closed. One non-urban cell; 78.1% of the province cannot be scored.
Persistence is rarely the referenceSkill against persistence is the headline number, and the mean of three is added as a harder reference.Closed at the sites studied.
Few studies explain their inputsThe four input sets show what radar and weather add. On L4, the inputs of the random forest were ranked.Partly closed.
Advanced models are used without a local baselineBenchmark first. No deep learning in this study.Closed at the sites studied. The thesis now has a number to beat.
Failures are rarely describedSkill split by wet and dry season on L3; errors by rainfall and wetness on L4.Partly closed.

How it was coded

In one lineOne Python script of 253 lines runs the whole benchmark. Smaller scripts before it fetch the data, and smaller scripts after it run the checks.

ภาษาไทยสั้น ๆ

  • โค้ดหลักคือไฟล์ Python ไฟล์เดียว ยาว 253 บรรทัด ชื่อ soil_moisture_l3_v3.py
  • สคริปต์ก่อนหน้าทำหน้าที่ดาวน์โหลดข้อมูล ส่วนสคริปต์ถัดไปทำหน้าที่ตรวจสอบผล
  • ทุกขั้นบันทึกผลเป็นไฟล์ CSV จึงตรวจย้อนได้ว่าตัวเลขแต่ละตัวในรายงานมาจากไหน

The files, in the order they run

  1. Fetch the satellite readings

    • download_smap_l3_province.py asks NASA for one month at a time, keeps every 9 km cell over the province with its quality flags, and throws the big files away. About 2 hours; it can resume.

    → data/raw/smap_l3_province_pathum_thani.csv

  2. Fetch the radar and the weather

    • extract_sentinel1_rtc.py reads only the window over the province from each radar scene and averages it over each cell. About 10 minutes.
    • l3_province_pixels.py ranks the cells, which is how cell (3,6) was chosen.
    • download_weather_point.py fetches daily weather for the chosen cell.

    → data/raw/sentinel1_rtc_province_pathum_thani.csv
    → data/raw/weather_era5seamless_px3_6.csv

  3. Run the benchmark

    • soil_moisture_l3_v3.py builds the inputs, trains and tests every forecaster year by year, and writes the scores. About 30 minutes.

    → code/results_l3_v3_main_px3_6.csv  (64 rows: 16 forecasters at 4 horizons)
    → …_pred.csv  (all 1,710 test forecasts)  ·  …_hyperparams.csv  (the settings picked)  ·  …_perfold.csv  (scores by test year)

  4. Run the checks

    • l3_real_data_evaluation.py: how the forecasts behave on the real record, such as after heavy rain.
    • l3_climatology_evaluation.py and l3_climatology_sensitivity.py: the same forecasts under other yardsticks.
    • l3_seed_sensitivity.py: 20 more random seeds for the tree models.
    • l3_extra_checks.py, l3_spatial_references.py, l3_nested_test.py: the later checks, including all 20 non-urban cells.

    Each one reads the saved forecasts and writes a small .json file of results.

  5. Write the report and the slides

    • The report is LaTeX in spacial_study_report/. The slides are built by build_seminar_deck.py, which stops if a number on a slide does not match a result file.

Inside the main script, in eight steps

The lines below are copied from the script unchanged. A line with only … marks lines left out. Grey text after # is a note in the script itself.

1. Load the readings and keep the recommended ones

Read the big table, pick one cell, keep quality flags 0 and 8, and take the morning reading first. The result, o, is a short table: one row per day that has a reading.

soil_moisture_l3_v3.py
p = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "data/raw/smap_l3_province_pathum_thani.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
p = p.drop_duplicates(["date", "pass", "yi", "xi"])
px = p[(p.yi == YI) & (p.xi == XI)].copy()
…
if A.quality == "recommended":
    px = px[px.qual.isin([0, 8])]
am = px[px["pass"] == "AM"].set_index("date").sm
pm = px[px["pass"] == "PM"].set_index("date").sm
s = pd.DataFrame({"am": am, "pm": pm}).sort_index()
if A.target == "am":   s["sm"] = s.am.where(s.am.notna(), s.pm)
elif A.target == "pm": s["sm"] = s.pm.where(s.pm.notna(), s.am)
else:                  s["sm"] = s[["am", "pm"]].mean(axis=1)
o = s.dropna(subset=["sm"]).reset_index()[["date", "sm"]]

2. Build the inputs from the readings

shift(k) means "the row k places above". Because the table holds only days with a reading, the row above is the previous reading, however many days ago it was. Its age is the difference between the two dates.

soil_moisture_l3_v3.py
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    o[f"sm_prev{k}"] = o.sm.shift(k)
    o[f"age_prev{k}"] = (o.date - o.date.shift(k)).dt.days
doy = o.date.dt.dayofyear
o["doy_sin"], o["doy_cos"] = np.sin(2*np.pi*doy/365.25), np.cos(2*np.pi*doy/365.25)

3. Add the weather windows and the latest radar scene

rolling(win) looks back over the last 3, 7 or 30 days. merge_asof with direction="backward" finds, for each reading day, the most recent radar scene on or before it, never a later one.

soil_moisture_l3_v3.py
for win in (3, 7, 30):
    w[f"rain{win}"] = w.rain.rolling(win).sum()
    w[f"temp{win}"] = w.temp.rolling(win).mean()
    w[f"rad{win}"]  = w.rad.rolling(win).mean()
soil_moisture_l3_v3.py
o = pd.merge_asof(o.sort_values("date"), s1, left_on="date", right_on="s1_date", direction="backward")
o["s1_age"] = (o.date - o.s1_date).dt.days

4. Name the four input sets

HIST is the nine inputs from the readings. The other sets add radar (S1), weather (MET), or both.

soil_moisture_l3_v3.py
HIST = ["sm"] + [f"sm_prev{k}" for k in (1, 2, 3)] + [f"age_prev{k}" for k in (1, 2, 3)] + ["doy_sin", "doy_cos"]
SETS = {"L3": HIST, "L3+S1": HIST + S1, "L3+met": HIST + MET, "L3+S1+met": HIST + S1 + MET}

5. Define the three models and the settings to try

Each grid is a short list of settings: 9 for the random forest, 18 for XGBoost, 4 for ridge. random_state=0 fixes the random seed so that a re-run gives the same trees.

soil_moisture_l3_v3.py
RF_GRID  = [{"max_depth": d, "min_samples_leaf": l} for d in (None, 10, 20) for l in (1, 5, 10)]
XGB_GRID = [{"learning_rate": lr, "max_depth": md, "subsample": ss}
            for lr in (0.03, 0.06, 0.1) for md in (3, 5, 7) for ss in (0.7, 1.0)]
RIDGE_GRID = [{"alpha": a} for a in (0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0)]
def make(kind, g):
    if kind == "rf":  return RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1, **g)
    if kind == "xgb": return XGBRegressor(n_estimators=500, colsample_bytree=0.8, random_state=0,
                                          n_jobs=-1, verbosity=0, **g)
    return make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(**g))

6. Pick the settings by a rehearsal, then refit

inner marks the last training year. Each setting is fitted on the earlier years and tried on that year. The best one is then fitted again on all the training years.

soil_moisture_l3_v3.py
def tune_fit(kind, X, y, inner):
    if inner.sum() < 20 or (~inner).sum() < 40:           # fall back to the last 20%
        inner = np.zeros(len(y), bool); inner[int(len(y)*0.8):] = True
    best, be = None, np.inf
    for g in GRIDS[kind]:
        e = rmse(y[inner], make(kind, g).fit(X[~inner], y[~inner]).predict(X[inner]))
        if e < be: best, be = g, e
    return make(kind, best).fit(X, y), best

7. Walk forward year by year and collect every forecast

For each horizon, y is the reading exactly h days later. Rows without a full set of inputs and an answer are dropped, so every forecaster is tested on the same rows. Then each year in turn becomes the test year: train on the years before it (tr), forecast it (te).

soil_moisture_l3_v3.py
for h in HORIZONS:
    x = o.copy(); x["y"] = [lookup.get(d + pd.Timedelta(days=h), np.nan) for d in x.date]
    …
    x = x.dropna(subset=ALLF + ["y"]).reset_index(drop=True)
    yr = x.date.dt.year.values
    …
    for ty in sorted(np.unique(yr))[1:]:
        tr, te = yr < ty, yr == ty
        …
        if tr.sum() < 120 or te.sum() < 20: continue
        ytr = x.y.values[tr]
        …
        P["persistence"].append(x.sm.values[te])
        P["mean3"].append(x[["sm", "sm_prev1", "sm_prev2"]].values[te].mean(axis=1))
        …
        inner = yr[tr] == yr[tr].max()
        for sname, feats in SETS.items():
            X = x[feats].values
            for kind in ("ridge", "rf", "xgb"):
                mdl, g = tune_fit(kind, X[tr], ytr, inner)
                P[f"{kind}|{sname}"].append(mdl.predict(X[te]))

8. Score

sk is the skill against persistence and skm the skill against the mean of three. dm_test asks whether the difference could be luck, and block_boot gives a range for the skill.

soil_moisture_l3_v3.py
    for name in REFS + FIT:
        pr = S[name]; sk = 1 - rmse(t, pr)/bp; skm = 1 - rmse(t, pr)/bm
        …
        if name != "persistence":
            _, row["DM_p"] = dm_test(t-pers, t-pr, h)
            row["CI_lo"], row["CI_hi"] = block_boot(t, pers, pr, h)

Three safeguards written into the code

  • Same rows for everyone. A row is kept only if every input of the largest set and the answer exist (dropna(subset=ALLF + ["y"])). So a difference in skill is never a difference in the test data.
  • No look into the future. The radar is paired backward only, the weather windows end on the issue day, and the answer is always at least two days after the inputs.
  • Repeatable. Every random seed is 0, and the settings picked in every test year are saved. Refitting ridge from them reproduces the saved forecasts exactly.

How to run it

in a terminal, from the code/ folder
../.venv/bin/python download_smap_l3_province.py 2016-01-01 2024-12-31
../.venv/bin/python extract_sentinel1_rtc.py
../.venv/bin/python l3_province_pixels.py
../.venv/bin/python download_weather_point.py LAT LON px3_6
../.venv/bin/python soil_moisture_l3_v3.py --pixel 3,6 --weather px3_6 --save-pred --tag main_px3_6

The first step needs a NASA Earthdata login token, which is kept in a private file outside git. The full runbook, with every check, is code/README.md.

Tools. Python 3.14 with pandas 3.0, NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, scikit-learn 1.9 and XGBoost 3.4.

Which model wins?

In one lineThere is no single champion. The plain average of the last three readings does most of the work. At 8 days ridge regression makes about 6% less error than that average, and it is the one learned result that holds up.

Two rulers, two different questions

Every result in the report is measured with one of two rulers. Both turn an error into a share: how much smaller it is than a reference's error.

RulerThe question it answersRidge regression at 8 days
SkillHow much smaller is the error than that of persistence, "tomorrow equals today"? 1 − 0.03481 ÷ 0.03980 = +0.125, so about 12.5% less error
GainHow much smaller is the error than that of the mean of three, the plain average of the last three readings? 1 − 0.03481 ÷ 0.03705 = +0.060, so about 6% less error

The errors are shown to five decimals here so that the sums work out. Elsewhere they are rounded to four.

Why two rulers? Persistence is the easy ruler. The plain mean of three clears it at every horizon, and it needs no training at all. So a learned model earns its place only by beating that average. For a learned model the number that counts is the gain, not the skill.

First ruler: did they beat persistence?

Yes, on SMAP L3, the product this study forecasts. The table gives each method's skill against persistence. Above zero means less error than "tomorrow equals today". A shaded number is clearly above zero: the whole range the data allow for it (the 95% interval) lies above zero.

Skill against persistence2 days3 days5 days8 days
Seasonal normal
simple reference		−0.164+0.025−0.068−0.084
Damped persistence
simple reference		+0.008+0.133+0.054+0.089
Mean of three
simple reference		+0.147+0.204+0.144+0.069
Ridge regression
learned model		+0.106+0.238+0.136+0.125
Random forest
learned model		+0.070+0.237+0.172+0.144
XGBoost
learned model		−0.053+0.192+0.139+0.120
  • At 3, 5 and 8 days every method except the seasonal normal clearly beats persistence. Ridge removes 11 to 24% of persistence's error over the four horizons. The closest call is the mean of three at 8 days, whose range starts at +0.006.
  • At 2 days only the mean of three and ridge clearly do. With 203 test forecasts there, the other four cannot be told apart from persistence. That is not the same as being equal to it.
  • Two methods score below zero somewhere: the seasonal normal at 2, 5 and 8 days, and XGBoost at 2 days. Neither is clearly below, because those ranges include zero.
  • "No model beat persistence" is a different result. That sentence, on the first page and under Results, is about SMAP L4, the side study: a smoother product, at another point, at 1, 3 and 7 days. There the best learned model scored −0.131, −0.066 and −0.041 (report Table 4.6). L4 hardly changes from one day to the next (its day-to-day correlation is 0.987, report Table 4.7), so copying today's value leaves little for a model to add.

The 8-day race, on one ruler

Here are the typical errors at 8 days, lowest at the bottom. Read it as two steps down.

  • Step one, smoothing. Averaging the last three readings removes 7% of persistence's error. No learning is involved.
  • Step two, learning. Ridge removes another 6% of what is left. That second step is the gain, and it is the report's headline number.

Second ruler: the gain, horizon by horizon

The winner changes with how far ahead the forecast is. A gain only counts if it passes the strict test, which allows for the twelve comparisons made between the learned models and the mean of three.

Ridge's gain of +0.060 passes: adjusted p 0.022, and 0.024 in the purged run. The forest's error is lower still, but in the purged run its adjusted p rises to 0.12: its gain is sensitive to settings chosen on a single year.

So who is the champion?

  • PracticalThe mean of three. No learning and no settings. It is the best of all at 2 days and never more than 9% behind the lowest error at the other horizons. If you must pick one method to use, pick this one.
  • LearnedRidge regression at 8 days. A gain of +0.060 that passes in the main run (adjusted p 0.022) and in the purged run (0.024), counting the report's twelve comparisons. It is the only learned result that passes both. The report also picks ridge as the bar for the thesis because it has no random seed and its weights can be read directly.
  • Not crownedThe random forest. Lowest error at 5 and 8 days. But its 8-day gain (+0.081) fails in the purged run (adjusted p 0.12). A later check traced this to its settings, which are chosen on a single year. Count all 48 comparisons as one group instead, and the forest's main-run gain is the only 8-day gain that passes (0.033), while ridge's does not (about 0.10). So which model looks like the champion depends on the counting rule: say so if asked.
  • TiesThe one-number rule. Seasonal normal plus a fixed share of the recent departure scores as well as the learned models. It was found after the results were known, so it is a check, not a contender.
  • OpenRidge against damped persistence. At 8 days damped persistence is the best simple rule (0.0363 against 0.0371 for the mean of three). Ridge's error is lower again, but that difference has not been tested. Expect the question.

How big is the gain, really?

  • +0.060 is a share, not an amount of water. It says ridge removes 6% of the error that the plain average leaves.
  • In water it is about 0.002 m³/m³. A reading of 0.37 means 37% of the soil's volume is water, so the gain is about 0.2 of a percentage point, while the typical miss is still about 3.5 points.
  • It is close to the line. With a wider tuning range, tried afterwards, the adjusted p is 0.051. Counting all 48 comparisons as one group, it is about 0.10. Without 2024, the best year, the gain is +0.046. See how solid the main result is.
  • It is still positive in every check: in 6 of the 7 test years, and at all 20 non-urban cells.

One sentence for the seminar

"No single model wins. Averaging the last three readings does most of the work; at 8 days ridge regression makes about 6% less error than that average, a gain of +0.060, which passes the strict test but sits close to the line."

NextResults and limits

Judge it

Results and limits

In one lineThe gain from learning at 8 days is small, positive in every check, and close to the pass line of the strict test. The weakness is the data, not the models.

1. Smoothing does most of the work

The plain mean of three, with no learning, already beats persistence. So the fair question is not "does a model beat persistence?" but "does it beat the mean of three?".

Why would a plain average win? A single reading can jump and then come back. Persistence copies the jump. The average of three damps it.

2. Learning adds a small gain at 8 days

This chart shows only what ridge regression adds on top of the mean of three. At 8 days it adds +0.060. In real units that is about 0.002 m³/m³.

The random forest's 8-day gain is larger (+0.081), but a later check showed that it is sensitive to settings chosen on a single year. That is why ridge regression is the headline model.

A test made for this kind of comparison, run last, adds one point. At 5 days there is something to learn beyond the plain average, but ridge regression did not turn it into a better forecast. At 2 days the test finds nothing to learn.

3. Radar and weather add nothing measurable

Adding Sentinel-1 radar, weather, or both changed the skill of ridge regression and the random forest by at most 0.02 at 2, 3 and 5 days, and by −0.025 to +0.004 at 8 days. The chart is under What each model adds.

4. Wetting after heavy rain is not forecast

When more than 20 mm of rain fell inside the 3-day window, the soil reading rose by +0.017 on average. The forecasts barely moved (−0.002 to +0.004). Also, much of the 3-day gain comes from ignoring single readings that jump and come back.

5. A one-number rule is hard to beat

Take the normal value for the time of year, and keep 70 to 82% of how far the recent average is from normal. That rule scores as well as the learned models. It was defined after seeing the results, so it is a check on the study, not a proposed model.

Separately, on SMAP "L4". L4 is a smooth, model-filled product. On it, no model beat persistence at 1, 3 or 7 days. That is about L4 only. On L3, the product behind the five findings above, every method except the seasonal normal clearly beats persistence at 3, 5 and 8 days (see the table). L4 is a different product and place, so the two are not compared directly.

How solid is the main result?

The main positive result is ridge regression's 8-day gain of +0.060. It was checked in many ways. The fair summary: small, positive in every check, and close to the pass line of the strict test.

  • PassesThe benchmark as specified: adjusted p = 0.022 (twelve comparisons).
  • PassesThe same run without a few borderline training pairs: adjusted p = 0.024.
  • PassesA different target (the average of the morning and evening readings): gain +0.067, adjusted p = 0.004.
  • SupportsPositive in 6 of the 7 test years. Negative only in 2018, the year with the least training data.
  • SupportsPositive at all 20 non-urban cells of the province, with p below 0.05 at 15 of them (not adjusted).
  • SupportsA test built for "nested" models, run last: the readings hold something the plain average does not use at 3, 5 and 8 days (one-sided p at most 0.0003), and nothing it can detect at 2 days. It asks a different question, so it does not make the gain bigger.
  • Just missesWith a wider tuning range, tried afterwards: gain +0.057, adjusted p = 0.051.
  • MissesIf all 48 comparisons are counted as one group: adjusted p about 0.10.
  • WeakerWithout 2024, the year of the largest gain: +0.046, p = 0.023 (not adjusted).

What it means for a user

  • The useful, simple message: average the last three readings. Learned models add very little on top.
  • The error that remains is about 0.03 m³/m³, roughly two thirds of the signal's own spread. It is measured against the satellite reading, not against the ground.
  • The satellite product is listed with a 50-hour delay. So of the 2-, 3-, 5- and 8-day horizons, about 0, 1, 3 and 6 days would really remain.

The honest limits

  1. One cell. Its sensed area is about 36 by 47 km. Only 53 to 59% of that lies inside the province, and about 41% lies on squares flagged urban.
  2. No ground sensors. Thailand has no public soil-moisture network, so nothing here is proven against the true soil moisture.
  3. The wettest days are missing, although floods are part of the motivation.
  4. Small samples. 203 to 639 test forecasts per horizon.
  5. The headline result is close to the threshold, as the list above shows.
NextWhy these choices

Judge it

Why these choices

In one lineEvery choice of data, place, horizon, input and setting has a stated reason. Most were forced by what the satellite record allows.

The order of work

The study follows a fixed order of questions. Each stage must be settled before the next one starts.

  • Data before scores. A skill score means little until you know where the readings are good. That decides where a forecast can be scored, and how many days ahead.
  • Simple forecasts before learned ones. Skill is always measured against a reference. The references must be fixed first, or a model gets credit for what a plain average would do anyway.
  • Inputs before models. An input earns its place only if it adds something beyond the references.

Said openly in the report. The work did not follow this order from the start. The first benchmark was run on L4, before the quality of L3 had been examined. Some choices were made after results were known, and the report names each one.

The data problem came first

SMAP marks each reading with a quality flag. Only "recommended" readings were used. That one rule decides where a forecast can be scored at all.

  • The quality rule. SMAP withholds its "recommended" mark when the sensed area is more than 25% urban or more than 5% open water, when rain is heavier than 1 mm an hour, or when vegetation is dense. NASA's own validation uses the same mark. Across the 53 grid cells of the scan, the rule keeps 27.2% of the readings.
  • The cell. Cell (3,6) was picked by three plain rules: never flagged urban, at least 90% inside the province, and the most recommended days among the cells that qualify (981, against 946 for the other one).
  • What the rule costs. It throws away mostly wet-season readings. A usable reading exists on 36 to 40% of days from January to April, but on only 10% of October days.

Keep these two apart. The province-wide result is the quality scan only. The forecasting results are for the selected cell, never "for the province".

Which data, and why

SMAP L3

Role
The target: the thing being forecast.
Why chosen
It is the satellite's own reading. The earlier target, L4, is filled in by a model and is very smooth (one day matches the next at 0.987), so "tomorrow equals today" could not be beaten there. The advisor approved L3 on 23 September 2026.
Limit
A usable reading on only 29.8% of days, and none in cells flagged urban.

Sentinel-1 radar

Role
An extra input.
Why chosen
A second satellite view of the surface, at 10 m. The question was whether it adds anything beyond the readings.
Limit
559 usable scene-days. The grid cell it is averaged over is much smaller than the area SMAP senses, so radar and target do not describe the same ground.

Weather reanalysis (ECMWF)

Role
An extra input.
Why chosen
Rainfall, temperature and sunlight: what wets and dries the soil. It has no gaps, all 3,288 days.
Limit
A model estimate for an area of about 27 km, not a rain gauge. Irrigation and field flooding are in no input.

SMAP L4

Role
The earlier target, kept as a comparison.
Why chosen
It has a value on every day.
Limit
Model-filled, a different area and different horizons (1, 3 and 7 days). Not a direct comparison with L3.

MERRA-2 and ECMWF soil moisture

Role
Comparison only.
Why chosen
To compare products with SMAP. The report calls this product intercomparison.
Limit
It is not validation: none of them is the ground truth.

Left out

GLDAS
It had no working download route.
Ground sensors
Thailand has no public soil-moisture network.

Why 2, 3, 5 and 8 days

The proposal said 1, 3 and 7 days. That assumes a reading every day. SMAP passes over this cell on three days out of every eight, so two readings are 2, 3 or 5 days apart, or 8.

  • The test needs at least 120 training pairs and 20 test pairs in every test year. 41 pairs over nine years cannot give that, so 1 and 7 days are out.
  • 6 days had enough pairs. It was left out of the benchmark to keep the same horizons as the earlier analysis, and run later as a check.
  • Each horizon gets its own model. A one-step model is not repeated, because that adds up its own errors.

What goes into a forecast

The time line of one forecast is under How a forecast is made. These are the three groups of inputs and the reason each is built the way it is.

Readings: 9 inputs

What is in it
The latest reading; the three before it; how many days old each of those three is; the season, as the day of the year.
Why built this way
Readings come at uneven gaps, so columns such as "one day ago" cannot be filled. The ages tell the model whether an earlier reading is two days old or eight.

Radar: 3 inputs

What is in it
The brightness of the latest scene in two channels (VV and VH), and the age of that scene.
Why built this way
Only a scene on or before the issue date, covering at least half the cell. A later scene would let the future in. In the middle case the scene is 2 days old.

Weather: 9 inputs

What is in it
Total rain, mean temperature and mean sunlight, each over the last 3, 7 and 30 days.
Why built this way
So that a recent shower, a wet week and a wet month can all count. The three windows were not tuned.
  • The latest reading is always an input. Persistence uses it. A model without it would be solving a harder problem than the reference it is scored against.
  • Gaps are never filled in. A filled value leans on the reading after the gap, which is the future. The inputs are counted in readings, not in calendar days.

The settings, and how they were chosen

Models are always tested on a year they have never seen. Their settings are chosen inside the training years only.

Ridge regression

Fixed
Inputs put on one scale.
Tried in each test year
Strength of the penalty: 0.1, 1, 10 or 100.
What was picked
The strongest, 100, in 69 of 108 fits. A range up to 10,000 was tried later and improved nothing.

Random forest

Fixed
300 trees.
Tried in each test year
Depth of the trees: unlimited, 10 or 20. Smallest leaf: 1, 5 or 10 pairs.
What was picked
The largest leaf in 43 of 108 fits.

XGBoost

Fixed
500 trees.
Tried in each test year
Learning rate: 0.03, 0.06 or 0.1. Depth: 3, 5 or 7. Share of pairs each tree sees: 0.7 or 1.0.
What was picked
The lowest learning rate in 54 of 108 fits, the greatest depth in 50.
  • Why so few values? The settings are picked on one held-out year of 25 to 113 pairs. A big search on so few pairs would pick noise.
  • What the picks say. Ridge most often took the strongest penalty and XGBoost the slowest learning rate, each at the edge of its range. The report says this shows where the ranges were narrow. For ridge a wider range was tried and did not help.
  • Other numbers that were fixed, not tuned: three readings in the mean of three; 7 days either side for the seasonal normal; weather windows of 3, 7 and 30 days; random seed 0, with 20 more seeds run as a check.

Present it

For the seminar

In one lineTwo sentences to keep ready, the papers to name, what changed on 10 and 11 November, and what to do next.

Two sentences to keep ready

On the main result: "It is small, it is positive in every check I ran, in six of seven years and at all 20 non-urban cells, and it sits close to the threshold of the strict test."

On the study as a whole: "The weakness is the data, not the models: one noisy cell, no ground truth, the wettest days removed. The strength is the fair test."

Which papers to highlight

The report cites 71 references. These carry the argument. If you can name only five, name the first five.

PaperWhat it gives youOne sentence to say
Entekhabi et al. 2010The SMAP mission paper. The 0.04 m³/m³ design requirement."0.04 is a target for the satellite reading against the ground. My errors are against the reading, so I use it only as a familiar scale."
Chan et al. 2018The enhanced product: a 9 km grid, but a sensed area of about 36 by 47 km. A 50-hour delay."Nine kilometres is the grid spacing, not what the satellite sees."
Ganepola et al. 2026The AIT roadmap. No SMAP validation site exists in Mainland Southeast Asia."This is why I say product intercomparison and never validation."
Murphy 1988 and 1992A skill score needs a simple reference, and the reference should be the best simple method."A model is only good compared with something simple."
Gruber et al. 2020The community's rules for checking soil-moisture products, including how to compute the seasonal normal."My seasonal normal is shorter than the guidance asks, so I repeated the comparisons under seven definitions."
Jotisankasa et al. 2023The only check of SMAP against buried sensors in Thailand (R² 0.13 to 0.58 after monthly averaging)."The one Thai comparison shows moderate agreement."
Seneviratne 2010; Orth and Seneviratne 2013Soil moisture has memory of days to weeks."The textbooks say the soil remembers. At my cell one reading was a weak predictor; the average of several was not."
Fang and Shen 2020The closest earlier work: deep learning that forecasts SMAP L3 itself one to three days ahead. It does not compare with persistence."The closest study reports good errors but never asks whether it beats persistence or a simple average."
Shellito et al. 2016; McColl et al. 2017The layer SMAP senses dries fast: a median drying time of 4.08 days for SMAP against 7.33 days for buried probes; about 14% of rain is still held after three days."The surface layer forgets rain within days, which fits what I found."
Wang et al. 202413 models at 30 stations: deep learning beats a random forest only narrowly at short leads."A baseline study with simple models is a fair place to start."
Carranza et al. 2021A random forest matched a physics model at 15 Dutch stations."A random forest is a legitimate benchmark."

The gap to state. Of the 21 studies compared in the report, none reports skill against persistence, none tests the model comparison for significance, none compares L3 with L4 as forecast targets, and none is set in the tropics. The 21 were chosen to represent each generation of methods, not by a systematic search.

The full list, with a line for each paper, is in spacial_study_report/literature_highlights.md.

Every number in this guide is in the report or in its result files. Forecasting results are for the selected SMAP L3 cell in Pathum Thani, checked at other non-urban cells; they are not a result for the province.
